newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Wheat volatile on weather, copper consolidates.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Wheat volatile on weather, copper consolidates.

text.p: World wheat prices were volatile on Friday, pushed down by rain in North America and in parched areas of Europe but supported by varied crop damage estimates after a recent freeze in the US Great Plains.

Elsewhere in world commodity markets copper held steady at higher levels and was seen consolidating after spiking higher over much of the week. Coffee futures slumped sharply lower, erasing early London gains.
Wheat prices moved slightly higher in what was seen as a technical recovery to a late break on Thursday, supported by forecasts for heavy rainfall in US Great Plains hard red winter wheat region.
Chicago Board of Trade soft red winter wheat futures for May were off Thursday's highs but up 2-1/2 cents on the day at $4.24 a bushel.

But trade was seen remaining volatile amid a variety of estimates about the recent freeze damage which sparked a surge in wheat prices last week to values above $4.50 and forecasts for continuing rainfall in England and France after a prolonged dry spell in much of Europe.

Snow fell in the Texas Panhandle early on Friday and forecasts called for nearly a foot of snow in that region which could further damage wheat hurt by last week's freezing weather, independent forecasters Weather Services Corp said.
An export tax on soft wheat grain and flour announced by the EU on Thursday also helped to push the market higher.

"The export levy is aimed at dampening prices on the EU market and to ensure sufficient control on exports to avoid any shortages developing," European Commission agriculture spokesman Gerard Kiely told a news briefing.

Copper prices finished the day slightly higher and traders said they expected the market to consolidate for a while, but saw it remaining underpinned as long as a strike at Chile's big Escondida mine continued and London Metal Exchange stocks remained on a downward trend.
Labour unrest served to emphasise near-term supply concerns as some workers at Escondida, the world's largest copper mine, voted on Wednesday to continue with their strike.
Copper for three months delivery ended the day firmer at around $2,383 per tonne.

Coffee prices in London dropped sharply after a relatively strong start in London's morning amid news that the six-day old truck drivers' strike in Colombia, the world's secodn largest coffe producer, was on the verge of ending.

"We're still working out a few points but everything is basically agreed," said union leader Javier Suarez, adding that the union would wait until President Ernesto Samper had signed a final accord before ordering drivers back to work.
Coffee futures of the robusta type for May delivery in London closed $19 lower at $1,590 a tonne, just off the day's low of $1,585.

Coffee futures in New York headed lower at the open pressured by the news of an imminent end to the Colombian truck drivers' strike, but trader said persistent supply concerns and positive technical indicators helped the market bounce back.
July arabica futures in New York were up 0.05 cent at 198.25 cents per lb at midday.

World oil prices corrected lower in a quiet market on Friday after climbing late on Thursday on reports that United Nations staff in northern Iraq had been arrested by a Kurdish group. The U.N. later said the report was untrue.
"Most of Thursday's gains were on the Iraq rumours which turned out to be untrue so maybe now we're seeing more realistic levels," said one oil trader.
Benchmark North Sea Brent blend crude oil for June slipped back some 11 cents to trade around $18.31 in London's afternoon, having touched a high of $18.55.
Gold met selling when buyers tried to lift it out of the narrow range it has languished in for much of the last two weeks. It finished near the day's highs at $342.50, but still within its range.
